definition: A material with a large number of charge carriers that are free to move through it, such as the free electrons in a metal, so a potential difference produces a significant current.
A material whose electrons are bound to their atoms or molecules, so it has very few mobile charge carriers and the current in it is negligible.
The potential difference across a component divided by the current in it, $R = \frac{V}{I}$, measured in ohms ($\Omega$); it depends on the component's material, shape and temperature.
A property of a material, $\rho = \frac{RA}{L}$, measured in $\Omega\ \text{m}$, that sets how strongly it resists current whatever the length or thickness of the sample.
The current in a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided its temperature stays constant; it is not the definition of resistance.
A component that does not obey Ohm's law, so its I–V graph is not a straight line through the origin, such as a filament lamp or a light-emitting diode.
